facts.definition: The superficial layer of the skin: keratinized stratified squamous epithelium.
The deep layer of the skin: connective tissue with blood vessels, glands, hair follicles, and nerve endings.
Loose connective and adipose tissue beneath the dermis that anchors skin to underlying structures. Not part of the skin proper.
Thin superficial zone of areolar tissue in and near the dermal papillae; rich in small blood vessels and mobile defensive cells.
The deep, thick layer of dense irregular connective tissue; stretching it in obesity or pregnancy tears collagen and produces striae.
Deepest stratum: a single layer of cuboidal to low columnar keratinocytes on the basement membrane, with stem cells, melanocytes, and tactile cells. Stem cells here divide to replace the epidermis.
Several layers of keratinocytes; usually the thickest stratum (except on palms and soles). Deepest cells still divide; higher cells flatten and make keratin filaments.
3 to 5 layers of flat keratinocytes packed with coarse, dark-staining keratohyalin granules.
A thin, pale, featureless zone of densely packed keratinocytes found only in thick skin (palms, soles).
Up to 30 layers of dead, scaly, keratinized cells forming a durable surface resistant to abrasion, penetration, and water loss.
The part of the hair above the skin surface.
The part of the hair within the follicle, below the surface.
The swollen base of the hair root where the hair grows; contains the hair matrix and a dermal papilla.
The tube of epithelium and connective tissue surrounding the hair root.
Smooth muscle attached to the follicle; contraction makes the hair stand up (goose bumps).
A gland opening into the hair follicle that secretes oily sebum; overactivity at puberty causes acne.
The common sweat gland that opens by a duct onto the skin surface through a pore; cools the body.
A sweat gland in the axilla and groin that opens into a hair follicle and produces thicker secretions; active after puberty.
Finger-like upward projections of the dermis into the epidermis, carrying capillaries and touch receptors.
Downward folds of the epidermis between the dermal papillae; they produce fingerprints.
The opening of an eccrine sweat duct on the skin surface.
An oval receptor in the dermal papillae for light touch; dense in fingertips and lips.
A large onion-like receptor deep in the dermis or hypodermis for deep pressure and vibration.
Bare nerve fibers in the epidermis and dermis that sense pain, heat, and cold.
A receptor in the dermis for heavy, continuous pressure and skin stretch.
A receptor in mucous membranes (lips, tongue, genitals) for light touch.
Nerve fibers wrapped around a follicle that detect hair movement.
The main epidermal cell; produces keratin and is pushed upward from the stratum basale to be shed at the surface.
A cell in the stratum basale that makes melanin and passes it to keratinocytes.
A touch-sensing cell in the stratum basale linked to a nerve fiber.
An immune cell in the stratum spinosum and granulosum that captures invading microbes.
Skin with a thick stratum corneum and a stratum lucidum, and no hair; palms, soles, fingertips.
Skin with a thin stratum corneum, no stratum lucidum, and hair follicles; most of the body.
Damages only the epidermis; red, painful, no blisters; heals in days (sunburn).
Damages the epidermis and part of the dermis; blisters, very painful; epidermis regenerates from hair follicles and gland linings.
Destroys the epidermis, all of the dermis, and often deeper; can be painless at first because nerve endings are destroyed; needs grafting.
A follicle plugged with sebum and keratin that stays closed at the surface.
A plugged follicle open at the surface; the dark color is oxidized melanin and lipid, not dirt.
An inflamed, pus-filled lesion that forms when bacteria multiply in a plugged follicle.
The most common and least dangerous skin cancer; arises from the stratum basale; rarely spreads.
Arises from keratinocytes of the stratum spinosum; can spread if untreated.
Cancer of melanocytes; the most dangerous skin cancer; spreads early. Screened with the ABCDE rule.
Melanoma warning signs: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter over 6 mm, Evolving.

questions.prompt: You are given an unlabeled slide showing a very thick stratum corneum and a visible stratum lucidum. Is this thick or thin skin? Name two body locations it could have come from.
questions.modelAnswer: Thick skin. The stratum lucidum exists only in thick skin. Palms of the hands and soles of the feet (also fingertips).

questions.prompt: List the five strata of the epidermis from deep to superficial.
questions.modelAnswer: Stratum basale, stratum spinosum, stratum granulosum, stratum lucidum (thick skin only), stratum corneum.

questions.prompt: Of the hairy scalp, the axilla, and the sole of the foot, which is classified as thick skin, and which epidermal layer is responsible for that classification?
questions.modelAnswer: The sole of the foot. Thick skin is defined by a thick stratum corneum and the presence of the stratum lucidum. The scalp and axilla are thin, hairy skin; the axilla also has apocrine sweat glands.

questions.prompt: From what structures can the epidermis regenerate after a second-degree burn? What is different about a third-degree burn?
questions.modelAnswer: After a second-degree burn, new epidermis grows from the surviving epithelium lining hair follicles and sweat glands deep in the dermis. A third-degree burn destroys the whole dermis including those structures, so the skin cannot regenerate on its own and needs a graft.

questions.prompt: Why can a third-degree burn be less painful, at least initially, than a second-degree burn?
questions.modelAnswer: The third-degree burn destroys the nerve endings in the dermis, so the burned area itself cannot feel pain. A second-degree burn leaves the nerve endings alive and exposed.

questions.prompt: What actually causes the dark color of a blackhead?
questions.modelAnswer: Oxidation of the melanin and lipid in the plug exposed to air, not trapped dirt.

questions.prompt: Which gland is primarily responsible for acne, and what change at puberty increases the risk of developing it?
questions.modelAnswer: The sebaceous gland. Rising sex hormones (androgens) at puberty increase sebum production, which plugs follicles.

questions.prompt: What do the ABCDE criteria refer to?
questions.modelAnswer: Warning signs of melanoma: Asymmetry, Border irregularity, Color variation, Diameter greater than 6 mm, Evolving (changing) lesion.

questions.prompt: Why do the palms, soles, and fingertips differ so much in receptor density and epidermal thickness from the skin of your back or abdomen?
questions.modelAnswer: They take the most friction and are used for fine touch, so they have thick skin with a stratum lucidum for protection and dense tactile corpuscles for sensitivity. The back and abdomen have thin, hairy skin with fewer touch receptors.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to a keratinocyte as it moves from the stratum basale to the stratum corneum.
questions.modelAnswer: It is produced by stem cell division in the stratum basale, pushed upward, flattens and fills with keratin in the spinosum and granulosum, loses its nucleus and organelles, and finally becomes a dead, scale-like cell in the stratum corneum that is eventually shed.
